query: What prespecified descriptive estimands, CI methods, and clustering adjustments should a pilot use so its estimates meaningfully inform sample-size calculations for the definitive trial?

response.query: What prespecified descriptive estimands, CI methods, and clustering adjustments should a pilot use so its estimates meaningfully inform sample-size calculations for the definitive trial?
response.answer: Pilot studies should use confidence intervals for sample size, rely on clinically important differences, and adjust for clustering if necessary to inform definitive trial sample size.

results.title: (PDF) Considerations in Determining Sample Size for pilot Studies
results.content:
Title: (PDF) Considerations in Determining Sample Size for pilot Studies
1. Pilot studies should use sample sizes ranging from 10 to 40 participants per group for various aims. 2. Confidence intervals can determine appropriate sample sizes for pilot studies, enhancing statistical reliability. Sample size calculations is necessary for approval of research projects, clearance from ethical committees, approval of grant from funding bodies, publication requirement for journals and most important of all justify the authenticity of study results. It is mandatory to calculate sample size in any type of research in medical science to get a generalized conclusion for the population under study. The sample size is the number of patients or other experimental units that need to be included in a study to answer the research question. Objectives: To describe a method using confidence intervals (CIs) to estimate the sample size for a pilot randomized trial. Study Design: Using one-sided CIs and the estimated effect size that would be sought in a large trial, we calculated the sample size needed for pilot trials. The determination of the required sample size is always an important step during the planning of the quality of research for a quantitative study. The researchers need to have sound prerequisite knowledge of the inferential statistics concept for determining a minimum sample size requirement and its estimation because an insufficient sample size may not be able to answer the research questions and a large sample is wastage of resources, may add to the complexity, and take more time for the study. Therefore, this study provides researchers with appropriate sample size determination methods for quantitative study. This study presents the sample size calculation formula in a simplified manner with relevant examples so that researchers may effectively use them in their research. Some basic aspects of statistical methods and sample size determination in health science research. This article provides a brief overview of statistical methods used at various stages of a research study with the main emphasis on estimation of minimum sample size for various types of objectives. Background: The Pre-Consultation Educational Group Intervention pilot study seeks to assess the feasibility and inform the optimal design for a definitive randomized controlled trial that aims to improve the quality of decisionmaking in postmastectomy breast reconstruction patients.

results.title: Determining sample size for pilot trials: a tutorial
results.content: Because the goal of pilot trials is not to estimate or test intervention efficacy or effectiveness, traditional sample size calculations for definitive trials are not directly applicable.18 In practice, researchers frequently rely on rules of thumb, which might be suitable for some but not all pilot trials.1920 Sample size explanations are frequently absent in pilot trial reports.21. To ensure 95% confidence in observing at least one disagreement, the researchers calculate a sample size of 30 participants (15 per group for a two-group study, rounded up from 29 for 1:1 equal allocation) for the pilot trial (appendix 1 table 5). By definition, pilot trials have small sample sizes that result in imprecise estimates of effects, and pilot trials with promising results might be more likely to be published and cited in plans for definitive trials, so relying solely on effect point estimates from pilot trials can lead to suboptimal sample sizes for definitive trials.51525354 Rather, researchers should use clinically important differences between groups—informed by previous research and expert opinion—to determine effect sizes that should be used to calculate required sample sizes. To estimate variability for normally distributed outcomes, researchers can conduct a pilot trial with 12 or 35 participants per group to achieve reasonable precision and efficiency (appendix 2 box 1 includes more details).1137 Conservatively, the definitive trial’s sample size should be increased to mitigate the probability of being underpowered because the variability estimate comes from a small trial.38 When there is uncertainty in the variance estimate, blinded sample size re-estimation might be done after the definitive trial has started55; this approach uses the variance data collected during the trial to adjust the sample size as needed.56. In these studies, researchers establish targets for meaningful improvement and calculate the proportion of participants who meet those targets.14 In some contexts, researchers might conduct pilot trials of appropriate size to inform decisions about progression.42 This approach relies on the sample size calculation method proposed by Cocks and Torgerson42 that accounts for additional uncertainty in the effect size estimate. Determining sample size for pilot trials: a tutorial BMJ 2025; 390 :e083405 doi:10.1136/bmj-2024-083405.

results.title: Guidance for using pilot studies to inform the design of intervention trials with continuous outcomes - PMC
results.content: While review of clinical records can be used to give some indication of potential participant pool, pilot studies provide estimates of the number of participants that actually enroll and consent to randomization, and these estimates should be included in the manuscripts that report the pilot study results.9 Many trials struggle to reach their sample size goal, which can result in trial extensions or failure to recruit to their prespecified sample size.10 Failure to recruit is a major issue in UK publicly funded trials, where 45% fail to reach target sample size.10 Along with review of prior trials at the same centers in similar populations, pilot studies can also give estimates of retention rates and adherence rates.11 Missing data and dropouts are issues in most RCTs12 and need to be considered at each step of the research process,13 including design, reporting,9 and progression to a larger definitive trial.11,14. The target effect size must also be realistic, and the estimated effect size and confidence interval (CI) from the pilot can give some evidence here, ie, whether there is any indication that the intervention is effective and important differences might be obtained in the main trial.5 The small sample size of a pilot makes estimation uncertain, so caution must be exercised.19,20 One approach for handling this uncertainty is to use significance levels other than the “traditional” 5% to provide preliminary evidence for efficacy, with corresponding CIs such as 85 and 75% in addition to 95% CIs.21 A figure showing these CIs, the MID, and the null value can be a helpful way of displaying pilot results, by facilitating an assessment of both statistical significance and the potential for clinical significance.31 While some authors argue against carrying out hypothesis tests and assessing efficacy from pilots, even potential efficacy, most pilot studies do undertake hypothesis tests.6 We strongly stress that preliminary efficacy evidence from a pilot study should not be overstated, and researchers should avoid temptation to forgo the main trial.20,22. Whitehead et al27 showed how, if you know the main trial’s target effect size, you can estimate the pilot study’s optimum sample size, minimizing the number of patients recruited across the two studies.
